title: The brothers come for bread (Genesis 42)
hook: they bow to a man they don't recognize
carry: you don't see who it is

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's dreams: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner put in charge of Egypt's grain. Your line was store in the good years. Now the lean years arrive.

The famine spreads past Egypt, all the way to Canaan, to Jacob's tents. Jacob hears there's grain in Egypt. Why are you staring at each other? he asks his sons. Go down and buy us food, so we can live. Ten brothers go. Not Benjamin; Jacob won't let Rachel's last son out of his sight. So ten men walk into Egypt with money in their bags and stand before the governor who sells the grain to everyone. And they bow down to him, faces to the ground. Just like the sheaves in the dream they once hated him for.
screen: `THE FAMINE REACHES CANAAN.` → `TEN BROTHERS, NOT BENJAMIN.` → `FACES TO THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: The Torah puts the whole scene in one line: "And Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew him not." How could they miss him? He was seventeen when they sold him; now he's a grown man, shaved and dressed like an Egyptian, speaking through an interpreter. An old explanation, passed on by Rashi, puts it simply: when they sold him he had no beard, and now he had one. But there's a deeper reason. They weren't looking for him. You don't see who it is when you've decided who it can't be. Joseph remembers the dreams. He speaks to them harshly. The Hebrew is clever here: he recognized them, and made himself a stranger to them, two verbs from the same root. He calls them spies. They protest: we are twelve brothers, sons of one man; the youngest is with our father, and one is no more. One is no more. They're talking about him, to his face. Joseph keeps one brother, Simeon, as a hostage: bring me your youngest brother. Then, thinking the governor can't understand Hebrew, the brothers say to each other: "We are verily guilty concerning our brother." We saw his distress when he pleaded with us, and we wouldn't listen. Reuben says, didn't I tell you? And Joseph, who understands every word, turns away and weeps. All these years later, the brothers are finally talking about what they did, and the man they did it to is standing right there, listening.
screen: `JOSEPH KNEW THEM; THEY KNEW HIM NOT.` · `HE MADE HIMSELF A STRANGER.` · `ONE IS NO MORE.` · `WE ARE VERILY GUILTY.` · then, large: `HE TURNED AWAY AND WEPT.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've filed away: a difficult coworker, a relative you've written off, a stranger you decided about in one glance. Ask what you might not be seeing, what they might be carrying, or who they might have become since. You don't have to change your mind; just leave the door open a crack.
Simeon, the brother Joseph kept as a hostage in Egypt until the others returned with Benjamin.
Your line: you don't see who it is. They bowed to the brother they'd sold, and never knew him. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish commentators read this chapter as the start of the brothers' repair, the moment they admit aloud what they did to Joseph.

fork.setup: you're Joseph, governor of Egypt. the brothers who sold you are bowing in front of you, and they don't know who you are. what do you do?
options: tell them who you are at once.
hide who you are and test them.
have them thrown out of Egypt.
fork.reveal: he makes himself a stranger, calls them spies, keeps Simeon, and asks for Benjamin. when he hears them admit their guilt, he turns away and weeps.

original.note: Hebrew: he recognized them, and made himself a stranger. both from the root n-k-r.

what it means: they didn't see him because they'd decided he couldn't be there. and at last, they admit what they did.
what a scholar hears: 42:7 plays on n-k-r, recognize and estrange. Rashi on 42:8: he'd had no beard when sold, and now had one.

chat.says: How did Joseph's brothers stand right in front of him and not recognize him?
options: He'd grown up and looked Egyptian, and they'd decided it couldn't be him.
Joseph wore a mask at court, so nobody in Egypt ever saw his face.
They knew him, but pretended not to, out of fear of the governor.
chat.meaning: Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew him not. He'd changed, and you don't see who it is when you've decided who it can't be.

notes: 'Nearly forty': Joseph is 30 at 41:46, plus seven years of plenty and the start of famine, so about 37–38. Confirm.
Rashi on 42:8 (beard), from Yevamot 88a / Ketubot 27b. Confirm.
